## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Machine Learning for Time Series
  Official title       Apprentissage pour les séries temporelles
  Instructors          L. OUDRE (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 36 h (lectures 27 h, labs 9 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Signal processing
  Language             not displayed on the official pages
  Assessment           lab reports (25 %) and mini-projects: report 25 %, source code 25 %, oral defence 25 % (master-mva.com); non-integral continuous assessment, “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (Université Paris-Saclay course detail)
  Prerequisites        probability and statistics; basic notions of machine learning and signal processing (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics, who has met probability and a first course in machine learning, and who now faces data indexed by time — sensors, physiology, energy, economics.

**Empirical first**: on the synthetic Cylinder–Bell–Funnel benchmark, a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier with the Euclidean distance misclassifies about 13 % of the test series, and the same classifier with dynamic time warping misclassifies none of them (code of [ch. 3](#ch3)). The Euclidean distance compares sample $t$ with sample $t$, while the patterns that define the classes are shifted and stretched in time.

That small experiment is the whole course in miniature. A time series is not a vector of independent coordinates: neighbouring samples are dependent, patterns move, regimes change, values go missing, and several channels interact. Each chapter chooses a *representation* that takes the temporal structure into account — autocorrelations and spectra, linear dynamics, warping paths, sparse codes, segmentations, features, graphs — and turns it into an algorithm.

The page leans on the optimisation of [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) and the statistics of [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html). Its graph chapter opens the door to [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), and its detection chapter to [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Compute and interpret the autocorrelation, the periodogram, the spectrogram and the wavelet coefficients of a series.
-   Fit autoregressive and state-space models, forecast with them, and evaluate any forecaster without leaking the future.
-   Compare series with dynamic time warping, bound it from below, and build nearest-neighbour and shapelet classifiers.
-   Discover repeated motifs and isolated discords with the matrix profile.
-   Learn sparse and convolutional dictionaries that extract recurring patterns from long signals.
-   Segment a signal by penalised change-point detection (optimal partitioning, PELT, kernel costs) and choose the penalty.
-   Design and evaluate detectors for point, contextual and collective anomalies.
-   Denoise by Wiener filtering and wavelet thresholding, and impute missing values by splines, Kalman smoothing and low-rank completion.
-   Extract interpretable features from series and select them without selection bias.
-   Represent a multivariate series on a graph, filter and interpolate it, and learn the graph from the data.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com starts from applications (health, economics, advertising…) in which the collected data take the form of time series. The fundamental issue, it says, is to choose a representation that accounts as well as possible for the temporal information.

The course aims to give an overview of the machine-learning techniques used to study time series, for tasks such as pattern extraction and recognition, anomaly detection, prediction and interpolation. It is largely illustrated on real data and problems from current challenges, and insists on understanding and interpreting the data.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites (master-mva.com): probability and statistics, and basic notions of machine learning and signal processing.

-   **Refreshers** — [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (Gaussian vectors, conditional expectation, estimation), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (least squares, eigenvalues, gradient methods) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (every code block of this page).
-   **Related courses of the same semester** — [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (the lasso and proximal methods of ch. 4 and 7), [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (state-space models, Gaussian graphical models), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html), [Statistical Learning with Extreme Values](../s1-extreme-values/index.html) (rare events and anomalies), [Deep Learning and Signal Processing](../s1-deep-learning-signal-industry/index.html) and [Mathematical Methods for Neuroscience](../s1-neuroscience-maths/index.html).
-   **Courses that build on it in semester 2** — [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html), [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (kernel change-point costs), [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html), [Functional Brain Imaging and Brain–Computer Interfaces](../s2-brain-imaging-bci/index.html), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html) and [Biostatistics](../s2-biostatistics/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Review: probability, least squares and Fourier analysis** — Gaussian conditioning, ridge regression, the discrete Fourier transform and the convolution theorem.
-   **Representing a time series** — stationarity, autocorrelation, spectral density, periodogram, spectrogram, Haar wavelets, trend and seasonality.
-   **Linear models, state space and forecasting** — AR and ARMA models, Yule–Walker equations, best linear prediction, the Kalman filter, forecasting as supervised learning and its honest evaluation.
-   **Extracting and recognising patterns** — dynamic time warping and its lower bounds, nearest-neighbour classification, the matrix profile, shapelets.
-   **Sparse representations and dictionary learning** — OMP, ISTA and FISTA, recovery guarantees, MOD and K-SVD, convolutional sparse coding.
-   **Detecting changes and anomalies** — cost functions, optimal partitioning, PELT, kernel costs, penalties; anomaly types, residual, isolation and sequential detectors.
-   **Repairing data** — Wiener filtering, wavelet thresholding, missingness mechanisms, splines, Kalman smoothing, low-rank completion.
-   **Extracting and selecting relevant features** — interpretable features, random convolutional kernels, filter, wrapper and embedded selection.
-   **Multivariate series and graphs** — graph Fourier transform, graph filters, interpolation on a graph, learning the graph.
-   **Neural networks for time series** — dilated convolutions, recurrent networks and Transformers, and the baselines they must beat (self-study).
-   **Research directions and open problems** — foundation models, evaluation, irregular sampling, spatio-temporal graphs (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1 and check that Proposition 0.2 (Gaussian conditioning) and Theorem 0.5 (convolution theorem) feel familiar: ch. 2, 4, 6 and 8 use them without warning.
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in the *Practice* column, then rerun the code blocks of the chapter and change one parameter at a time.
-   Keep one notebook per lab; the lab reports count for 25 % of the official grade, so write the observations as you go.
-   Choose the mini-project early (session 8 at the latest): most subjects reuse a lab.
-   Python environment: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, NetworkX and PyTorch (CPU) suffice for every block; all data are synthetic, with fixed seeds.

## 0. Review: probability, least squares and Fourier analysis {#ch0}

Three M1 tools carry most of the course: conditioning of Gaussian vectors (prediction, Kalman filtering, imputation), least squares (autoregressions, dictionaries, features) and the discrete Fourier transform (spectra, convolutions, filters). This chapter states them in the form used later, with short proofs.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Mean, covariance, Gaussian vector]{.tag} For a random vector $X \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with finite second moments, the mean is $\mu = \mathbb{E}[X]$ and the covariance is
$$
\Sigma = \mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mu)(X - \mu)^\top\big],
$$
a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix.

$X$ is **Gaussian**, $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$, if every linear form $a^\top X$ is a real Gaussian variable. When $\Sigma$ is invertible, $X$ has the density
$$
p(x) = (2\pi)^{-d/2} \det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12 (x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\Big).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Best linear predictor and Gaussian conditioning]{.tag} Let $(X, Y)$ be a random vector with means $\mu_X, \mu_Y$, covariance blocks $\Sigma_{XX}, \Sigma_{XY}, \Sigma_{YY}$, and $\Sigma_{YY}$ invertible.

Among all affine functions of $Y$, the one that minimises the mean squared error of prediction of $X$ is

::: key
[Key result — best linear predictor]{.tag}
$$
\hat X = \mu_X + \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} (Y - \mu_Y),
$$
:::

with error covariance
$$
\Sigma_{XX} - \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} \Sigma_{YX}.
$$

If $(X, Y)$ is Gaussian, then $\hat X = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]$, and the conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ is Gaussian with this mean and this covariance.

::: proof
*Orthogonality.* The error $E = X - \hat X$ has mean zero and
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(E, Y) = \Sigma_{XY} - \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} \Sigma_{YY} = 0.
$$

*Optimality.* Any other affine predictor writes $\hat X + a + B(Y - \mu_Y)$. Its error is $E - a - B(Y - \mu_Y)$, whose second moment is that of $E$ plus a non-negative term, because $E$ is centred and uncorrelated with $Y$.

*Gaussian case.* $(E, Y)$ is Gaussian and uncorrelated, hence independent. So $X = \hat X + E$ given $Y$ is $\hat X$ plus an independent Gaussian of covariance $\mathrm{Cov}(E)$, which expands to the stated formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same orthogonality principle — the error is orthogonal to everything the predictor may use — gives the Yule–Walker equations (ch. 2), the Kalman filter (ch. 2) and the Wiener filter (ch. 6).

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Least squares and ridge regression]{.tag} Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Every minimiser of $\|Ax - b\|^2$ solves the normal equations $A^\top A x = A^\top b$.

For $\lambda > 0$ the ridge problem $\min_x \|Ax - b\|^2 + \lambda \|x\|^2$ has the unique solution
$$
x_\lambda = (A^\top A + \lambda I)^{-1} A^\top b.
$$

::: proof
The objective is a convex quadratic with gradient $2A^\top(Ax - b) + 2\lambda x$. Setting it to zero gives the two formulas. For $\lambda > 0$ the matrix $A^\top A + \lambda I$ is positive definite, hence invertible, and the objective is strictly convex. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Discrete Fourier transform]{.tag} For $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the DFT is
$$
\hat x_k = \sum_{t=0}^{n-1} x_t\, e^{-2i\pi k t / n}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, n - 1.
$$

The index $k$ corresponds to the frequency $k/n$ cycles per sample, or $k f_s / n$ hertz for a sampling rate $f_s$. The FFT computes all coefficients in $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ operations.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Convolution theorem and Parseval]{.tag} Let the circular convolution be
$$
(x \circledast y)_t = \sum_{s=0}^{n-1} x_s\, y_{(t - s) \bmod n}.
$$

Then, for every $k$,
$$
\widehat{x \circledast y}_k = \hat x_k\, \hat y_k, \qquad \sum_{t} |x_t|^2 = \frac1n \sum_k |\hat x_k|^2.
$$

::: proof
*Convolution.* Expand and substitute $u = t - s \bmod n$:
$$
\sum_t \sum_s x_s y_{t-s} e^{-2i\pi k t/n} = \sum_s x_s e^{-2i\pi k s/n} \sum_u y_u e^{-2i\pi k u/n}.
$$

*Parseval.* The vectors $e_k = (e^{2i\pi k t/n})_t$ are orthogonal with $\|e_k\|^2 = n$, and $\hat x_k = \langle x, e_k \rangle$. Expanding $x$ in this basis gives the identity. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A linear filtering, a cross-correlation or a sliding inner product therefore costs $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$. This speeds up the matrix profile (ch. 3) and convolutional sparse coding (ch. 4).

::: note
[Note 0.6 — Sampling and aliasing]{.tag} A continuous signal whose spectrum vanishes above $B$ hertz is determined by its samples taken at $f_s > 2B$ (Shannon–Nyquist). Below that rate, a frequency $f$ is indistinguishable from $f - f_s$: it *aliases*.

In practice, sensors filter before sampling, and a series analysed here is a sequence $x_t$, $t = 1, \dots, n$, with a known sampling rate. Irregular sampling is discussed in [ch. 10](#ch10).
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The best linear predictor makes the error orthogonal to the data; for Gaussian vectors it is the conditional expectation.
-   Least squares and ridge regression have closed forms; ridge is always well posed.
-   The DFT diagonalises circular convolution and preserves energy up to the factor $n$.
:::

## 1. Representing a time series: stationarity, spectra and scales {#ch1}

Before learning anything from a series, one must decide what to look at: the raw samples, their correlations across lags, their frequencies, or their variations at several scales. This chapter defines these representations, says when they are meaningful (stationarity) and how to estimate them.

### Time series as data

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Time series]{.tag} A (regularly sampled) **time series** is a finite sequence $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ with $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The sample $x_t$ is observed at time $t / f_s$, for a sampling rate $f_s$.

The series is **univariate** when $d = 1$ and **multivariate** when $d > 1$, with one coordinate per channel or sensor.

The statistical model is a stochastic process $(X_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of which $x$ is a finite realisation. A learning problem uses either one long series (forecasting, segmentation) or a data set of series $x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(N)}$, possibly of different lengths (classification, clustering).
:::

::: note
[Note 1.2 — The tasks of the course]{.tag} The official themes correspond to a handful of tasks:

-   *modelling and representing* a series — this chapter, [ch. 2](#ch2) and [ch. 4](#ch4);
-   *forecasting* its future values — [ch. 2](#ch2);
-   *recognising and extracting patterns*, classifying series — [ch. 3](#ch3), [ch. 4](#ch4) and [ch. 7](#ch7);
-   *detecting changes and anomalies* — [ch. 5](#ch5);
-   *repairing* a series: denoising and imputing missing values — [ch. 6](#ch6);
-   *exploiting the structure between channels* — [ch. 8](#ch8).

One warning holds for all of them: samples are dependent. A random train/test split mixes past and future, and statistics computed on the whole series leak information. Every evaluation in this course respects the order of time.
:::

### Stationarity and autocorrelation

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Weak stationarity, autocovariance]{.tag} A process $(X_t)$ with finite second moments is **weakly stationary** if its mean $\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mu$ does not depend on $t$ and its covariance depends only on the lag:
$$
\gamma(h) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_{t+h}, X_t) \quad \text{for all } t, h \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$

The function $\gamma$ is the **autocovariance**, and $\rho(h) = \gamma(h) / \gamma(0)$ the **autocorrelation** (ACF).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Properties of an autocovariance]{.tag} For a weakly stationary process:

-   $\gamma(-h) = \gamma(h)$ and $|\gamma(h)| \le \gamma(0)$;
-   $\gamma$ is positive semi-definite: for all $n$, all times $t_1, \dots, t_n$ and all $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$,

    $$
    \sum_{i,j} a_i a_j\, \gamma(t_i - t_j) \ \ge\ 0.
    $$

In particular the Toeplitz matrix $\Gamma_n = [\gamma(i - j)]_{i,j = 1}^{n}$ is positive semi-definite.

::: proof
*Symmetry*: $\gamma(-h) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_{t-h}, X_t)$, and shifting both times by $h$ gives $\mathrm{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h}) = \gamma(h)$.

*Bound*: by Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$
|\mathrm{Cov}(X_{t+h}, X_t)| \le \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_{t+h}) \mathrm{Var}(X_t)} = \gamma(0).
$$

*Positivity*: the double sum is $\mathrm{Var}\big(\sum_i a_i X_{t_i}\big) \ge 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Sample autocovariance and autocorrelation]{.tag} For observations $x_1, \dots, x_n$ with mean $\bar x$, and $0 \le h < n$,
$$
\hat\gamma(h) = \frac1n \sum_{t=1}^{n-h} (x_{t+h} - \bar x)(x_t - \bar x), \qquad \hat\rho(h) = \frac{\hat\gamma(h)}{\hat\gamma(0)}.
$$

The factor $1/n$ (not $1/(n-h)$) keeps the estimated Toeplitz matrix positive semi-definite. Under mild conditions $\hat\rho(h)$ is consistent. For a white noise, $\hat\rho(h)$ is approximately $\mathcal{N}(0, 1/n)$, which gives the bands $\pm 1.96/\sqrt n$ drawn on ACF plots.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.6 — Three reference processes]{.tag} Let $(\varepsilon_t)$ be i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2$.

-   *White noise* $X_t = \varepsilon_t$: $\gamma(0) = \sigma^2$ and $\gamma(h) = 0$ for $h \ne 0$.
-   *Random walk* $S_t = \varepsilon_1 + \dots + \varepsilon_t$: $\mathrm{Var}(S_t) = t\sigma^2$ grows with $t$, so $S$ is **not** stationary. Its increments $S_t - S_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t$ are.
-   *AR(1)* $X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with $|\phi| < 1$: the stationary solution (ch. 2) has

    $$
    \gamma(h) = \frac{\sigma^2 \phi^{|h|}}{1 - \phi^2}, \qquad \rho(h) = \phi^{|h|}.
    $$

For the AR(1), the stationary solution $X_t = \sum_{j \ge 0} \phi^j \varepsilon_{t-j}$ (proved in Proposition 2.2) makes $\varepsilon_t$ uncorrelated with every earlier value $X_{t-h}$, $h \ge 1$.

Multiplying the equation by $X_{t-h}$ and taking expectations gives $\gamma(h) = \phi\,\gamma(h-1)$ for $h \ge 1$. Taking variances gives $\gamma(0) = \phi^2 \gamma(0) + \sigma^2$. The two formulas above follow.

With $\phi = 0.7$: $\rho(1) = 0.7$, $\rho(2) = 0.49$, $\rho(3) = 0.343$. The code below recovers these values from 4096 samples.
:::

### Spectral representation

The autocovariance describes dependence across lags; its Fourier transform describes how the variance is spread over frequencies.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.7 — Spectral density]{.tag} Let $(X_t)$ be weakly stationary with $\sum_h |\gamma(h)| < \infty$. The function
$$
f(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{h \in \mathbb{Z}} \gamma(h)\, e^{-ih\omega}, \qquad \omega \in [-\pi, \pi],
$$
is continuous, even and **non-negative**. It determines the autocovariance:

::: key
[Key result — Wiener–Khinchin pair]{.tag}
$$
\gamma(h) = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{ih\omega} f(\omega)\, d\omega, \qquad f(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{h} \gamma(h) e^{-ih\omega}.
$$
:::

::: proof
*Inversion.* The series converges uniformly, so it may be integrated term by term. Since
$$
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{i(h-k)\omega}\, d\omega = 2\pi\, \mathbb{1}[h = k],
$$
only the term $k = h$ survives.

*Non-negativity.* Assume $\mu = 0$ and set
$$
f_n(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi n}\, \mathbb{E}\Big|\sum_{t=1}^n X_t e^{-it\omega}\Big|^2 \ \ge\ 0.
$$

Expanding the square and grouping the pairs $(s, t)$ by lag $h = s - t$ gives
$$
f_n(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{|h| < n} \Big(1 - \frac{|h|}{n}\Big) \gamma(h)\, e^{-ih\omega}.
$$

By dominated convergence (the weights are bounded by 1 and $\gamma$ is summable), $f_n(\omega) \to f(\omega)$, which is therefore $\ge 0$. Evenness follows from $\gamma(-h) = \gamma(h)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

White noise has a flat spectrum $f = \sigma^2 / (2\pi)$. The AR(1) of Example 1.6 has
$$
f(\omega) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi\,(1 - 2\phi\cos\omega + \phi^2)},
$$
which concentrates the variance at low frequencies when $\phi > 0$. It follows by summing the two geometric series of $\sum_h \phi^{|h|} e^{-ih\omega}$.

::: def
[Definition 1.8 — Periodogram]{.tag} At the Fourier frequencies $\omega_k = 2\pi k / n$, the **periodogram** of $x_1, \dots, x_n$ is
$$
I_n(\omega_k) = \frac{1}{2\pi n} \Big| \sum_{t=1}^n (x_t - \bar x)\, e^{-it\omega_k} \Big|^2 .
$$

It is the squared modulus of the DFT (Definition 0.4), rescaled. For $k \ne 0$ it equals
$$
I_n(\omega_k) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{|h| < n} \hat\gamma(h)\, e^{-ih\omega_k},
$$
so it is the plug-in estimator of $f$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.9 — The periodogram is not consistent]{.tag} Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.7, the bias $\mathbb{E}[I_n(\omega_k)] - f(\omega_k)$ tends to 0 uniformly over the Fourier frequencies $\omega_k \ne 0$. However, for an i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ white noise and $0 < k < n/2$,
$$
I_n(\omega_k) \sim \frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{\chi^2_2}{2},
$$
whose variance $(\sigma^2 / 2\pi)^2$ does not decrease with $n$.

::: proof
*Bias.* At a Fourier frequency $\omega_k \ne 0$, $\sum_t e^{-it\omega_k} = 0$, so subtracting $\bar x$ changes nothing and $\mathbb{E}[I_n(\omega_k)] = f_n(\omega_k)$, with $f_n$ as in the proof of Theorem 1.7. The bound
$$
|f_n(\omega) - f(\omega)| \le \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_h \min\Big(1, \frac{|h|}{n}\Big)\, |\gamma(h)|
$$
does not depend on $\omega$ and tends to 0.

*Variance.* For $0 < k < n/2$, the real and imaginary parts of $\sum_t \varepsilon_t e^{-it\omega_k}$ are Gaussian, centred, uncorrelated (orthogonality of cosines and sines at Fourier frequencies), each of variance $n\sigma^2/2$. Their squared sum divided by $n\sigma^2/2$ is a $\chi^2_2$, and $I_n = \frac{\sigma^2}{4\pi}\chi^2_2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The periodogram must therefore be smoothed. **Welch's method** cuts the series into $K$ overlapping windowed segments and averages their periodograms. The variance is divided by about $K$, and the frequency resolution, now set by the segment length, is coarser by the same factor.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import welch

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, phi = 4096, 0.7
eps = rng.standard_normal(n)
ar = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):                       # AR(1): x_t = 0.7 x_{t-1} + eps_t
    ar[t] = phi * ar[t - 1] + eps[t]
x = ar + 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.1 * np.arange(n))   # + a period-10 cycle

def acf(x, max_lag):                        # sample ACF (Definition 1.5)
    xc = x - x.mean()
    g = np.array([xc[: len(x) - h] @ xc[h:] for h in range(max_lag + 1)]) / len(x)
    return g / g[0]

print("sample ACF, lags 0-3:", acf(ar, 3).round(2))
print("theory 0.7^h        :", (phi ** np.arange(4)).round(2))
f, P = welch(x, fs=1.0, nperseg=250)        # averaged periodogram
print("frequency of the spectral peak:", f[np.argmax(P)], "cycle/sample")
```

The output gives the ACF $(1, 0.70, 0.49, 0.35)$ against the theoretical $(1, 0.70, 0.49, 0.34)$, and a spectral peak at
$$
f = 0.1 \text{ cycle per sample},
$$
the hidden period of 10 samples, invisible on the raw ACF of the noisy mixture.

### Time–frequency and multiscale representations

A spectrum averages over the whole series. Speech, gait or an electrocardiogram change over time, so one needs representations that are localised both in time and in frequency.

::: def
[Definition 1.10 — Short-time Fourier transform, spectrogram]{.tag} Let $w$ be a window of length $M$ (Hann, for instance) and $H$ a hop size. The STFT of $x$ is
$$
X(m, k) = \sum_{t} x_t\, w(t - mH)\, e^{-2i\pi k (t - mH) / M},
$$
and the **spectrogram** is $|X(m, k)|^2$: a periodogram of each windowed frame, with frames indexed by $m$.

A long window resolves close frequencies but blurs fast events; a short window does the opposite. The Gabor–Heisenberg inequality makes the trade-off unavoidable: the product of the time spread and the frequency spread of a window is bounded below by a universal constant.
:::

Wavelets resolve the trade-off differently: short windows for high frequencies, long ones for low frequencies. The simplest wavelet basis, Haar's, is enough to state the main facts.

::: def
[Definition 1.11 — Haar wavelet transform]{.tag} Let $n = 2^J$ and $a^{(0)} = x$. For $j = 1, \dots, J$ and $k = 0, \dots, n 2^{-j} - 1$, set
$$
a^{(j)}_k = \frac{a^{(j-1)}_{2k} + a^{(j-1)}_{2k+1}}{\sqrt 2}, \qquad d^{(j)}_k = \frac{a^{(j-1)}_{2k} - a^{(j-1)}_{2k+1}}{\sqrt 2}.
$$

The Haar transform of $x$ is the vector $W x = (a^{(J)}, d^{(J)}, \dots, d^{(1)})$. The coefficient $d^{(j)}_k$ measures the variation of $x$ at scale $2^j$ around the time $k 2^j$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.12 — The Haar transform is orthonormal and fast]{.tag} $W$ is an orthogonal matrix, so
$$
\|Wx\| = \|x\|, \qquad x = W^\top (Wx),
$$
and both $Wx$ and $W^\top c$ cost $\mathcal{O}(n)$ operations: fewer than $4n$ additions and multiplications.

::: proof
Each level applies the orthogonal matrix
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}
$$
to disjoint pairs of entries. Level $j$ is thus orthogonal on the current approximation and the identity on the details already computed. A product of orthogonal maps is orthogonal.

Level $j$ processes $n 2^{-j}$ pairs, so there are $\sum_{j \ge 1} n 2^{-j} = n - 1$ pairs in all. Each pair costs two additions and two multiplications by $1/\sqrt 2$, hence fewer than $4n$ operations. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A piecewise-constant signal has nonzero Haar details only near its jumps: few large coefficients carry it. This *sparsity* is what wavelet denoising exploits in ch. 6.

### Trend and seasonality

Many series are a slow **trend** plus a periodic **seasonal** component plus a stationary remainder, $x_t = m_t + s_t + r_t$. Differencing removes the first two.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.13 — Differencing]{.tag} Let $\nabla x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}$ and $\nabla_p x_t = x_t - x_{t-p}$.

-   If $m_t$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ in $t$, then $\nabla^k m_t$ is constant and $\nabla^{k+1} m_t = 0$.
-   If $s_t$ is $p$-periodic, then $\nabla_p s_t = 0$.
-   If $r$ is stationary with spectral density $f_r$, then $\nabla r$ is stationary with density

    $$
    f_{\nabla r}(\omega) = |1 - e^{-i\omega}|^2 f_r(\omega) = (2 - 2\cos\omega)\, f_r(\omega).
    $$

::: proof
*Polynomials.* $t^k - (t-1)^k = k t^{k-1} + (\text{lower degree})$, so $\nabla$ lowers the degree by exactly one; after $k$ steps a constant remains, killed by one more step.

*Periodic part.* $s_t - s_{t-p} = 0$ by definition.

*Spectrum.* Expanding the covariance of the differences,
$$
\gamma_{\nabla r}(h) = 2\gamma_r(h) - \gamma_r(h+1) - \gamma_r(h-1).
$$
Inserting $\gamma_r(h) = \int e^{ih\omega} f_r$ gives the factor $2 - e^{i\omega} - e^{-i\omega}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Differencing thus removes trends but amplifies high frequencies: it should be used once or twice, not by reflex.

::: ex
[Example 1.14 — Removing a trend and a season]{.tag} Let $x_t = 1 + 0.5\,t + s_t$ with the period-4 season $s = (2, 0, -2, 0, 2, 0, -2, 0, \dots)$. For $t = 0, \dots, 7$:
$$
x = (3,\ 1.5,\ 0,\ 2.5,\ 5,\ 3.5,\ 2,\ 4.5).
$$

Seasonal differencing gives, for $t = 4, \dots, 7$,
$$
\nabla_4 x_t = (2, 2, 2, 2) = 4 \times 0.5,
$$
a constant, and one more ordinary difference gives 0. On real data the remainder $r_t$ survives these operations and is what the models of ch. 2 describe.

Robust alternatives estimate the trend by a centred moving average of length $p$ and the season by averaging each phase, or use the loess-based STL procedure of Cleveland and coauthors (1990).
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   Stationarity makes the autocovariance a function of the lag only; it is even, bounded by $\gamma(0)$ and positive semi-definite.
-   The spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance and is non-negative.
-   The raw periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but not consistent; average it (Welch).
-   Spectrograms and wavelets localise frequencies in time; the Haar transform is orthonormal and costs $\mathcal{O}(n)$.
-   Differencing removes polynomial trends and periodic seasons but amplifies high frequencies.
:::

## 2. Linear models, state space and forecasting {#ch2}

To forecast a series, or to fill its gaps, one needs a model of how the present depends on the past. This chapter builds the linear one: autoregressions, their optimal predictors, the state-space form with the Kalman filter, and then forecasting as ordinary supervised learning with an honest evaluation.

### Autoregressive and moving-average models

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — AR, MA and ARMA models]{.tag} Let $(\varepsilon_t)$ be a white noise of variance $\sigma^2$ and $B$ the backshift operator, $B x_t = x_{t-1}$. With the polynomials
$$
\phi(z) = 1 - \phi_1 z - \dots - \phi_p z^p, \qquad \theta(z) = 1 + \theta_1 z + \dots + \theta_q z^q,
$$
an **ARMA($p$, $q$)** process satisfies
$$
\phi(B) X_t = \theta(B) \varepsilon_t .
$$

The case $q = 0$ is the **autoregression** AR($p$), the case $p = 0$ the **moving average** MA($q$).

The process is **causal** if $X_t = \sum_{j \ge 0} \psi_j \varepsilon_{t-j}$ with $\sum_j |\psi_j| < \infty$: it depends on present and past shocks only. When $\phi$ and $\theta$ have no common zeros, this holds if and only if $\phi(z) \ne 0$ for $|z| \le 1$ (Brockwell and Davis, 1991). Its spectral density is then
$$
f(\omega) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi} \frac{|\theta(e^{-i\omega})|^2}{|\phi(e^{-i\omega})|^2}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — The AR(1) model]{.tag} The equation $X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ has a stationary solution if and only if $|\phi| \ne 1$. For $|\phi| < 1$ the solution is causal and unique:
$$
X_t = \sum_{j \ge 0} \phi^j \varepsilon_{t-j}, \qquad \gamma(h) = \frac{\sigma^2 \phi^{|h|}}{1 - \phi^2}.
$$

::: proof
*Uniqueness.* Iterating the equation $k$ times gives
$$
X_t = \phi^k X_{t-k} + \sum_{j < k} \phi^j \varepsilon_{t-j}.
$$
For a stationary solution, the second moment of $\phi^k X_{t-k}$ is $\phi^{2k}\, \mathbb{E}[X_0^2] \to 0$, so $X_t$ is the $L^2$ limit of the partial sums.

*Existence and covariance.* The series converges in $L^2$ since $\sum_j \phi^{2j} < \infty$. For $h \ge 0$, independence of the shocks gives
$$
\gamma(h) = \sigma^2 \sum_{j \ge 0} \phi^j \phi^{j+h} = \frac{\sigma^2 \phi^h}{1 - \phi^2}.
$$

*The case $\phi = \pm 1$.* Then $X_t - \phi^k X_{t-k}$ has variance $k\sigma^2$, while for a stationary process it is at most $4\gamma(0)$: impossible for large $k$. (For $|\phi| > 1$ a stationary but non-causal solution exists, written with future shocks.) [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Yule–Walker equations]{.tag} Let $X$ be a causal AR($p$). Then, for every $h \ge 1$,

::: key
[Key result — Yule–Walker equations]{.tag}
$$
\gamma(h) = \sum_{j=1}^p \phi_j\, \gamma(h - j), \qquad \sigma^2 = \gamma(0) - \sum_{j=1}^p \phi_j \gamma(j).
$$
:::

In matrix form, $\Gamma_p \boldsymbol\phi = \boldsymbol\gamma_p$, with the Toeplitz matrix $\Gamma_p = [\gamma(i - j)]_{i,j=1}^p$ and the vector $\boldsymbol\gamma_p$ of the autocovariances at lags 1 to $p$.

::: proof
Multiply $X_t = \sum_j \phi_j X_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t$ by $X_{t-h}$ and take expectations (centred process).

For $h \ge 1$, causality makes $X_{t-h}$ a function of $\varepsilon_s$, $s \le t - h$, hence uncorrelated with $\varepsilon_t$: the last term vanishes.

For $h = 0$, $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t X_t] = \sigma^2$, because $X_t - \varepsilon_t$ depends only on past shocks. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Replacing $\gamma$ by the sample autocovariance (Definition 1.5) gives the **Yule–Walker estimator**
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\phi} = \hat\Gamma_p^{-1} \hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_p .
$$

The $1/n$ normalisation keeps $\hat\Gamma_p$ positive definite, and the fitted model is always causal. The estimator is consistent and asymptotically Gaussian; least squares on the lagged values is asymptotically equivalent.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Optimal linear prediction of an AR($p$)]{.tag} For a causal AR($p$) and any $k \ge p$, the best linear predictor of $X_{t+1}$ from $X_t, \dots, X_{t-k+1}$ is
$$
\hat X_{t+1 \mid t} = \sum_{j=1}^p \phi_j X_{t+1-j},
$$
with mean squared error $\sigma^2$. The $h$-step predictor follows the recursion
$$
\hat X_{t+h \mid t} = \sum_{j=1}^p \phi_j \hat X_{t+h-j \mid t}, \qquad \hat X_{s \mid t} = X_s \ \text{for } s \le t.
$$

::: proof
The error of the proposed predictor is $\varepsilon_{t+1}$, uncorrelated with every $X_s$, $s \le t$, by causality. By the orthogonality principle (Proposition 0.2), the predictor is optimal, and its error is $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_{t+1}) = \sigma^2$.

For $h > 1$, project the model equation at time $t + h$ on the past: projection is linear, and the projection of $\varepsilon_{t+h}$ is zero. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Forecasting an AR(1)]{.tag} Take $\phi = 0.8$, $\sigma^2 = 1$ and the last observation $x_t = 2$. The recursion gives $\hat x_{t+h \mid t} = 0.8^h \times 2$, and the error of the $h$-step forecast is
$$
\mathrm{MSE}_h = \sigma^2 \sum_{j < h} \phi^{2j} = \sigma^2 \frac{1 - \phi^{2h}}{1 - \phi^2}.
$$

| Horizon $h$ | 1 | 2 | 5 | $\infty$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Forecast | 1.6 | 1.28 | 0.66 | 0 |
| MSE | 1 | 1.64 | 2.48 | 2.78 |

The forecast decays to the mean and its error grows to the variance $\gamma(0) = 1/0.36$: beyond a few correlation times, the model knows nothing more than the marginal law. A Gaussian 95 % interval at $h = 1$ is $1.6 \pm 1.96$.
:::

::: note
[Note 2.6 — ARIMA, seasonal models, exponential smoothing]{.tag} An **ARIMA($p, d, q$)** model says that $\nabla^d X$ is a causal ARMA($p, q$): differencing (Proposition 1.13) handles polynomial trends. Seasonal ARIMA adds $\nabla_s$ and polynomials in $B^s$. The book of Bisgaard and Kulahci (2011), in the official references, works through such models on real data.

**Simple exponential smoothing** forecasts with the level $\ell_t = \alpha x_t + (1 - \alpha)\ell_{t-1}$. It is the optimal predictor of an ARIMA(0, 1, 1) model, and the Holt–Winters variants add a trend and a season. Orders are chosen by an information criterion (AIC) on the Gaussian likelihood, which the Kalman filter below computes.
:::

### State-space models and the Kalman filter

The state-space form writes every linear model — AR, ARMA, trend plus season, several sensors — as a hidden Markov chain observed with noise. One algorithm then forecasts, filters, smooths and handles missing values (ch. 6).

::: def
[Definition 2.7 — Linear Gaussian state-space model]{.tag} A hidden state $s_t \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and an observation $y_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ follow
$$
s_{t+1} = F s_t + w_t, \qquad y_t = H s_t + v_t,
$$
with $w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q)$, $v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)$ and $s_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, P_0)$, all independent.

An AR($p$) is the case $s_t = (x_t, \dots, x_{t-p+1})$, with the companion matrix $F$ (first row $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_p$, ones below the diagonal), $H = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$ and $R = 0$.

The *local level* model $s_{t+1} = s_t + w_t$, $y_t = s_t + v_t$ is a random walk seen through noise.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.8 — Kalman filter]{.tag} Let $m_{t \mid t-1}, P_{t \mid t-1}$ be the mean and covariance of $s_t$ given $y_{1:t-1}$, and $m_{t \mid t}, P_{t \mid t}$ those given $y_{1:t}$. The conditional laws are Gaussian, and:

-   *prediction*: $m_{t \mid t-1} = F m_{t-1 \mid t-1}$ and $P_{t \mid t-1} = F P_{t-1 \mid t-1} F^\top + Q$;
-   *update*: with the innovation covariance $S_t = H P_{t \mid t-1} H^\top + R$ and the gain $K_t = P_{t \mid t-1} H^\top S_t^{-1}$,

    $$
    m_{t \mid t} = m_{t \mid t-1} + K_t\,(y_t - H m_{t \mid t-1}), \qquad P_{t \mid t} = (I - K_t H)\, P_{t \mid t-1}.
    $$

::: proof
By induction on $t$. Given $y_{1:t-1}$, $s_{t-1}$ is Gaussian with the filtered moments, and $s_t = F s_{t-1} + w_{t-1}$ with $w_{t-1}$ independent of everything before: this gives the prediction step.

Still given $y_{1:t-1}$, the pair $(s_t, y_t)$ is Gaussian with $\mathrm{Cov}(s_t, y_t) = P_{t \mid t-1} H^\top$ and $\mathrm{Var}(y_t) = S_t$, because $v_t$ is independent. Proposition 0.2 applied to this pair is exactly the update step. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The innovations $y_t - H m_{t \mid t-1}$ are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, S_t)$ variables, so the likelihood of the whole series is a product of $n$ Gaussian densities; maximising it fits $F$, $Q$ and $R$. The **Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother** adds a backward pass that conditions on the whole series:
$$
m_{t \mid n} = m_{t \mid t} + J_t\,(m_{t+1 \mid n} - m_{t+1 \mid t}), \qquad J_t = P_{t \mid t} F^\top P_{t+1 \mid t}^{-1}.
$$

It follows from Proposition 0.2 applied to $(s_t, s_{t+1})$ given $y_{1:t}$, and from the Markov property: given $s_{t+1}$, the state $s_t$ is independent of $y_{t+1:n}$. Chapter 6 uses it to impute gaps.

### Forecasting as supervised learning

::: def
[Definition 2.9 — Lag embedding, recursive and direct strategies]{.tag} Fix a number of lags $L$. The **lag embedding** turns a series into a regression data set with inputs $z_t = (x_{t-1}, \dots, x_{t-L})$ and targets $x_t$. Calendar variables and exogenous series can be appended to $z_t$.

Any regressor (ridge, gradient boosting, a neural network) then forecasts one step ahead. For a horizon $h$, the *recursive* strategy feeds its own forecasts back as inputs. The *direct* strategy trains one model per horizon on the targets $x_{t+h-1}$. The recursive strategy accumulates its errors; the direct one ignores the dependence between horizons and needs $h$ models.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.10 — Rolling-origin evaluation and forecast metrics]{.tag} Choose forecast origins $T_1 < T_2 < \dots < T_K$. For each $k$, fit the model on $x_{1:T_k}$ only and score its forecasts of $x_{T_k + 1 : T_k + H}$. The average score over origins is the **rolling-origin** (or time-series cross-validation) estimate.

Usual scores are the MAE, the RMSE and the scaled error **MASE**: the MAE divided by the in-sample MAE of the naive forecast $\hat x_{t+1} = x_t$ (Hyndman and Koehler, 2006). MASE below 1 beats the naive forecast. The percentage error MAPE explodes near zero values and should be avoided there.
:::

::: note
[Note 2.11 — Why a shuffled split is optimistic]{.tag} With a random split, a test point has its neighbours $x_{t-1}$ and $x_{t+1}$ in the training set; when residuals are correlated, they carry part of its value, and the score is optimistic. Bergmeir, Hyndman and Koo (2018) show that ordinary $K$-fold cross-validation remains valid for purely autoregressive models with uncorrelated errors. Outside that case, use a rolling origin.

Always report the naive and the seasonal naive forecasts ($\hat x_{t+h} = x_{t+h-s}$) as baselines.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import toeplitz, solve
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2000
x = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(2, n):                       # AR(2) with phi = (0.6, -0.3)
    x[t] = 0.6 * x[t - 1] - 0.3 * x[t - 2] + rng.standard_normal()

def yule_walker(x, p):                      # Theorem 2.3 with sample autocovariances
    xc = x - x.mean()
    g = np.array([xc[: len(x) - h] @ xc[h:] for h in range(p + 1)]) / len(x)
    phi = solve(toeplitz(g[:p]), g[1:])
    return phi, g[0] - phi @ g[1:]

phi_hat, s2_hat = yule_walker(x[:1000], 2)
print("Yule-Walker on the first 1000 points:", phi_hat.round(3), round(s2_hat, 3))

L = 5                                       # lag embedding: row t holds x_{t-1}, ..., x_{t-5}
X = np.column_stack([x[L - k - 1 : n - k - 1] for k in range(L)])
y = x[L:]
mse = {"naive (last value)": [], "AR(2) Yule-Walker": [], "ridge on 5 lags": []}
for origin in range(1000, len(y), 100):     # rolling origin (Definition 2.10)
    te = slice(origin, origin + 100)
    phi, _ = yule_walker(x[: origin + L], 2)            # refit on the past only
    ridge = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(X[:origin], y[:origin])
    mse["naive (last value)"].append(np.mean((y[te] - X[te, 0]) ** 2))
    mse["AR(2) Yule-Walker"].append(np.mean((y[te] - X[te, :2] @ phi) ** 2))
    mse["ridge on 5 lags"].append(np.mean((y[te] - ridge.predict(X[te])) ** 2))
for name, v in mse.items():
    print(f"{name:20s} one-step MSE = {np.mean(v):.3f}")
```

The estimate is $\hat{\boldsymbol\phi} = (0.578, -0.297)$ for the true $(0.6, -0.3)$. The one-step errors are 1.567 for the naive forecast, 1.055 for the AR(2) model and 1.060 for the ridge regression on 5 lags.

Both models come close to the floor
$$
\sigma^2 = 1
$$
of Theorem 2.4. The remaining gap of about 0.05 is within the sampling error of an average over about 1000 test points, whose standard deviation is close to $\sqrt{2/1000} \approx 0.045$. On a linear process, a flexible regressor cannot beat the right linear model; it can only match it.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   A causal AR($p$) has autocovariances given by the Yule–Walker equations, and its optimal one-step predictor is the model equation itself, with error $\sigma^2$.
-   Forecast errors grow with the horizon up to the variance of the series.
-   The Kalman filter is Gaussian conditioning applied recursively; the RTS smoother conditions on the whole series.
-   Forecasting is supervised learning on lag embeddings, evaluated with a rolling origin against naive baselines.
:::

## 3. Extracting and recognising patterns {#ch3}

Two heartbeats, two steps of a walker or two spoken words are "the same pattern" even when one is shifted, slower or locally stretched. This chapter builds distances that tolerate such deformations, uses them to classify series, and then searches long series for repeated patterns (motifs) and for short discriminative ones (shapelets).

### Comparing two series

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — z-normalisation and lock-step distances]{.tag} The **z-normalisation** of $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is $\hat x = (x - \bar x \mathbf{1}) / s_x$, where $\bar x$ is the mean and $s_x$ the standard deviation of its entries. It removes offset and amplitude, which are rarely what defines a pattern.

The Euclidean distance $\|x - y\|$ is a **lock-step** distance: it compares $x_t$ with $y_t$ only. A pattern shifted by a few samples, or played slightly faster, can be far from itself in this distance.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Warping path and dynamic time warping]{.tag} Let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$. A **warping path** is a sequence of index pairs $(i_1, j_1), \dots, (i_K, j_K)$ such that:

-   it starts at $(1, 1)$ and ends at $(n, m)$;
-   each step $(i_{k+1} - i_k,\ j_{k+1} - j_k)$ is $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$ or $(1, 1)$.

The **DTW** distance is the cost of the best path:
$$
\mathrm{DTW}(x, y) = \min_{\text{paths}} \Big( \sum_{k=1}^{K} (x_{i_k} - y_{j_k})^2 \Big)^{1/2}.
$$

The **Sakoe–Chiba band** of half-width $w$ restricts paths to $|i_k - j_k| \le w$; it forbids pathological alignments and speeds up the computation.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Dynamic programming for DTW]{.tag} Let $D(0, 0) = 0$, $D(i, 0) = D(0, j) = +\infty$ for $i, j \ge 1$, and

::: key
[Key result — the DTW recursion]{.tag}
$$
D(i, j) = (x_i - y_j)^2 + \min\big\{ D(i-1, j),\ D(i, j-1),\ D(i-1, j-1) \big\}.
$$
:::

Then $D(i, j)$ is the smallest cost of a warping path from $(1, 1)$ to $(i, j)$, and
$$
\mathrm{DTW}(x, y)^2 = D(n, m),
$$
computed in $\mathcal{O}(nm)$ time, or $\mathcal{O}(nw)$ with a band.

::: proof
By induction on $i + j$. A path ending at a pair $(i, j) \neq (1, 1)$ has its last-but-one pair among the three predecessors $(i-1, j)$, $(i, j-1)$ and $(i-1, j-1)$. Its cost is the cost of its prefix plus $(x_i - y_j)^2$.

The prefix is a path to that predecessor, so its cost is at least $D$ of the predecessor; and the optimal path to the best predecessor, extended by one step, attains the bound. Each of the $nm$ cells is filled in constant time. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — A shifted bump]{.tag} Let $x = (0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0)$ and $y = (0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0)$, the same bump one sample earlier. The Euclidean distance is
$$
\|x - y\| = \sqrt{0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0} = 2.
$$

The path $(1,1), (2,1), (3,2), (4,3), (5,4), (6,5), (6,6)$ matches equal values everywhere, so
$$
\mathrm{DTW}(x, y) = 0 .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — DTW is not a metric]{.tag} DTW is symmetric and non-negative, but $\mathrm{DTW}(x, y) = 0$ does not imply $x = y$, and the triangle inequality fails.

::: proof
*Zero distance.* $(0, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$ are at DTW distance 0: the last value of the first series is matched twice.

*Triangle inequality.* Take $x = (0)$, $y = (1)$, $z = (1, 1)$. The only path from $x$ to $z$ matches 0 with both ones, so
$$
\mathrm{DTW}(x, z) = \sqrt 2 \ >\ \mathrm{DTW}(x, y) + \mathrm{DTW}(y, z) = 1 + 0.
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Metric indexing structures therefore do not apply directly; fast search relies on lower bounds instead.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — The LB_Keogh lower bound]{.tag} Let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and a band of half-width $w$. Define the envelope of $y$ by
$$
U_i = \max_{|k - i| \le w} y_k, \qquad L_i = \min_{|k - i| \le w} y_k,
$$
and let $\mathrm{LB}(x, y)^2$ be the sum over $i$ of the squared distance from $x_i$ to the interval $[L_i, U_i]$. Then
$$
\mathrm{LB}(x, y) \ \le\ \mathrm{DTW}_w(x, y),
$$
and $\mathrm{LB}$ costs $\mathcal{O}(n)$.

::: proof
Every index $i$ appears in at least one pair $(i, j)$ of the optimal banded path, with $|i - j| \le w$, hence $y_j \in [L_i, U_i]$. The cost of that pair is at least the squared distance from $x_i$ to the interval.

Choosing one such pair for each $i$ selects distinct pairs of the path, so the sum of these lower bounds is at most the total cost. Running minima and maxima give the envelope in linear time. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In a nearest-neighbour search, a candidate whose lower bound exceeds the best distance found so far is discarded without computing DTW. The bound is presented in Keogh and Ratanamahatana (2005); cascades of such bounds let DTW search scale to trillions of subsequences (Rakthanmanon and coauthors, 2012).

::: note
[Note 3.7 — Averaging and differentiating DTW]{.tag} Clustering with $k$-means needs an average under DTW. *DTW barycentre averaging* (Petitjean and coauthors, 2011) alternates between aligning every series to the current average and averaging the aligned values.

*Soft-DTW* (Cuturi and Blondel, 2017) replaces the $\min$ of Theorem 3.3 by the smooth minimum $-\gamma \log \sum_i e^{-a_i / \gamma}$. The result is differentiable, its gradient is computed by a backward recursion of the same cost, and it can serve as a training loss.
:::

### Nearest-neighbour classification

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.8 — Cover and Hart (1967)]{.tag} Let the training pairs be i.i.d. in a separable metric space, with $K$ classes, and let $R^*$ be the Bayes error. Under mild regularity of the class-conditional laws, the error $R$ of the 1-nearest-neighbour rule tends, as the sample grows, to a limit that satisfies
$$
R^* \ \le\ R \ \le\ R^*\Big(2 - \frac{K}{K-1} R^*\Big) \ \le\ 2R^*.
$$

::: proof
Out of scope; see Cover and Hart (1967). The key step is that the nearest neighbour converges to the query point, so its label is an independent draw from the same conditional law. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

DTW is not a metric, so the theorem is only a guide. Empirically, 1-NN with a DTW whose band is tuned by cross-validation was long the baseline to beat on the UCR archive of time-series classification data sets (Dau and coauthors, 2019). The large comparison of Bagnall and coauthors (2017) found that many published methods were not significantly more accurate than this baseline.

The Cylinder–Bell–Funnel data set (Saito, 1994) is synthetic: a plateau, a ramp up or a ramp down, of random start, length and height, in Gaussian noise. The code generates it and compares the two distances.

```python
import numpy as np

def cbf(n_per_class, rng, length=128):      # Cylinder-Bell-Funnel (Saito, 1994)
    t, X, y = np.arange(length), [], []
    for label in range(3):
        for _ in range(n_per_class):
            a = rng.integers(16, 33)
            b = a + rng.integers(32, 97)
            chi = ((t >= a) & (t <= b)).astype(float)
            shape = [chi, chi * (t - a) / (b - a), chi * (b - t) / (b - a)][label]
            X.append((6 + rng.standard_normal()) * shape + rng.standard_normal(length))
            y.append(label)
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)

def dtw_to_all(q, C, w):
    """DTW between q and every row of C (squared costs, band half-width w)."""
    n, N = len(q), len(C)
    D = np.full((n + 1, n + 1, N), np.inf)
    D[0, 0] = 0.0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                # recursion of Theorem 3.3
        for j in range(max(1, i - w), min(n, i + w) + 1):
            best = np.minimum(np.minimum(D[i - 1, j], D[i, j - 1]), D[i - 1, j - 1])
            D[i, j] = (q[i - 1] - C[:, j - 1]) ** 2 + best
    return np.sqrt(D[n, n])

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
Xtr, ytr = cbf(10, rng)                      # 30 training series
Xte, yte = cbf(30, rng)                      # 90 test series
z = lambda X: (X - X.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / X.std(1, keepdims=True)
Xtr, Xte = z(Xtr), z(Xte)

d_euc = ((Xte[:, None, :] - Xtr[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
d_dtw = np.array([dtw_to_all(q, Xtr, w=12) for q in Xte])
for name, d in [("Euclidean", d_euc), ("DTW, 10% band", d_dtw)]:
    print(f"1-NN {name:14s} error = {np.mean(ytr[d.argmin(1)] != yte):.3f}")
```

With 30 training series, the Euclidean 1-NN errs on 13.3 % of the test series and the DTW 1-NN on none:
$$
\text{error}_{\text{Euclid}} = 0.133, \qquad \text{error}_{\text{DTW}} = 0.000 .
$$

### Motifs and discords: the matrix profile

In a single long series, one asks which pattern repeats (a *motif*) and which stretch resembles nothing else (a *discord*). The matrix profile answers both questions at once.

::: def
[Definition 3.9 — Matrix profile, motif, discord]{.tag} Let $T$ be a series of length $n$ and $T_{i,m} = (T_i, \dots, T_{i+m-1})$ its subsequences of length $m$.

Let $d_{i,j}$ be the Euclidean distance between the z-normalised subsequences $T_{i,m}$ and $T_{j,m}$.

The **matrix profile** is
$$
P_i = \min_{j\,:\,|i - j| \ge m/2} d_{i,j},
$$
the distance from each subsequence to its nearest non-trivial match. The exclusion zone $|i - j| < m/2$ discards a subsequence's overlapping copies of itself.

The pair $(i, j)$ that attains $\min_i P_i$ is the top **motif**. The index $\arg\max_i P_i$ is the top **discord**, a natural anomaly candidate (ch. 5).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.10 — Distance and correlation]{.tag} For subsequences $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with Pearson correlation $\rho(a, b)$, z-normalised with the population standard deviation,
$$
\|\hat a - \hat b\|^2 = 2m\,\big(1 - \rho(a, b)\big).
$$

::: proof
A z-normalised vector has mean 0 and $\|\hat a\|^2 = m$. Hence $\|\hat a - \hat b\|^2 = 2m - 2\langle \hat a, \hat b \rangle$, and $\langle \hat a, \hat b \rangle = m\,\rho(a, b)$ by definition of the correlation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

All distances therefore follow from the sliding dot products $\langle T_{i,m}, T_{j,m} \rangle$ and from sliding means and standard deviations (cumulative sums). For a fixed $i$, the dot products with all $j$ form one cross-correlation, computed by FFT (Theorem 0.5). Along a diagonal they update in constant time:
$$
\langle T_{i+1,m}, T_{j+1,m} \rangle = \langle T_{i,m}, T_{j,m} \rangle - T_i T_j + T_{i+m} T_{j+m}.
$$

This gives the exact matrix profile in $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n)$ memory (Yeh and coauthors, 2016; Zhu and coauthors, 2016). The block below uses the $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$-memory version, which is enough for 2000 samples.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, m = 2000, 50
T = np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n)) * 0.1 + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n)
motif = 2 * np.sin(np.linspace(0, 3 * np.pi, m))
for pos in (300, 1400):                      # plant the same pattern twice
    T[pos : pos + m] += motif

S = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(T, m)        # all subsequences
Z = (S - S.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / S.std(1, keepdims=True)
corr = Z @ Z.T / m                                         # Pearson correlations
dist = np.sqrt(np.maximum(2 * m * (1 - corr), 0))          # Proposition 3.10
idx = np.arange(len(Z))
dist[np.abs(idx[:, None] - idx[None, :]) < m // 2] = np.inf   # exclusion zone
P = dist.min(1)                                            # the matrix profile
i = int(np.argmin(P))
j = int(np.argmin(dist[i]))
print("motif pair (start indices):", sorted((i, j)), " distance:", round(P[i], 2))
print("discord (most isolated subsequence) starts at:", int(np.argmax(P)))
```

The top motif is the pair of subsequences starting at 302 and 1402, two samples after the planted copies (the z-normalised pattern matches best with a small offset). The discord, at index 63, is simply the most unusual stretch of the random walk: on a series without a planted anomaly, the top discord is not an anomaly.

### Shapelets

A class can be defined by a short pattern that appears *somewhere* in the series. Shapelets are such patterns, cut out of the training data.

::: def
[Definition 3.11 — Shapelet and shapelet distance]{.tag} A **shapelet** is a short series $s \in \mathbb{R}^L$. Its distance to a series $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge L$, is the distance to the best-matching window:
$$
\mathrm{sd}(s, x) = \min_{1 \le t \le n - L + 1} \frac1L \sum_{k=1}^{L} (x_{t+k-1} - s_k)^2 .
$$

A small $\mathrm{sd}(s, x)$ means that $s$ occurs in $x$, wherever it is: the distance is invariant to the position of the pattern.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.12 — Shapelet transform (Hills and coauthors, 2014)]{.tag} Given labelled training series:

1.  take as candidates the subsequences of the training series, for a range of lengths;
2.  score each candidate by how well its distances $\mathrm{sd}(s, x^{(i)})$ separate the classes — information gain, or an $F$-statistic;
3.  keep the $k$ best candidates, discarding those that overlap a better one;
4.  map every series $x$ to the vector of its $k$ shapelet distances, $\mathrm{sd}(s_j, x)$ for $j = 1, \dots, k$, and train any classifier on these vectors.
:::

With $N$ series of length $n$, there are about $N n^2 / 2$ candidates, each compared with $N$ series at a cost of order $n^2$. Exhaustive search is thus of order $N^2 n^4$ operations, which is why practical versions subsample the candidates or learn the shapelets by gradient descent (Grabocka and coauthors, 2014). The original shapelets of Ye and Keogh (2009) were used inside a decision tree.

The reward is interpretability: a shapelet is a piece of real data that one can plot and show to a domain expert.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
tri = np.r_[np.linspace(0, 2, 10), np.linspace(2, 0, 10)]   # class-1 pattern
sq = np.r_[np.zeros(3), 2 * np.ones(14), np.zeros(3)]      # class-0 pattern

def make(n, length=100):                    # pattern at a random position + noise
    X, y = 0.5 * rng.standard_normal((n, length)), rng.integers(0, 2, n)
    for k in range(n):
        p = rng.integers(0, length - 20)
        X[k, p : p + 20] += tri if y[k] else sq
    return X, y

def sdist(s, X):                            # shapelet distance (Definition 3.11)
    W = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(X, len(s), axis=1)
    return ((W - s) ** 2).mean(-1).min(-1)

def quality(d, y):                          # separation of the two classes
    a, b = d[y == 0], d[y == 1]
    return (a.mean() - b.mean()) ** 2 / (a.var() + b.var())

Xtr, ytr = make(40)
Xte, yte = make(300)
cands = [x[p : p + 20] for x in Xtr[:10] for p in range(0, 81, 2)]
scores = [quality(sdist(s, Xtr), ytr) for s in cands]
best = [cands[i] for i in np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:5]]   # keep the 5 best
F = lambda X: np.column_stack([sdist(s, X) for s in best]) # shapelet transform
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(F(Xtr), ytr)
print("shapelet transform + logistic regression, accuracy:", round(clf.score(F(Xte), yte), 3))
d = ((Xte[:, None, :] - Xtr[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
print("Euclidean 1-NN on the raw series, accuracy:      ", round(np.mean(ytr[d.argmin(1)] == yte), 3))
```

The patterns sit at random positions, so the lock-step 1-NN reaches only 0.67, while five shapelets learned from 40 series give
$$
\text{accuracy} = 0.917 .
$$

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   DTW aligns two series by the cheapest monotone warping path, computed by dynamic programming in $\mathcal{O}(nm)$, or $\mathcal{O}(nw)$ within a band.
-   DTW is not a metric; lower bounds such as LB_Keogh make nearest-neighbour search fast.
-   1-NN with DTW is a strong classification baseline.
-   The matrix profile finds motifs and discords from z-normalised distances, which reduce to correlations.
-   Shapelets classify by the presence of a local pattern anywhere in the series, and remain interpretable.
:::

## 4. Sparse representations and dictionary learning {#ch4}

A recurring pattern — a heartbeat, a step, a spike — can be seen as an *atom* that the signal uses a few times. This chapter represents signals as sparse combinations of atoms, learns the atoms from the data, and then makes the representation shift-invariant with convolutions, which turns it into a pattern-extraction tool.

### Sparse coding

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Dictionary and sparse coding]{.tag} A **dictionary** is a matrix $D = [d_1, \dots, d_K] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times K}$ whose columns, the **atoms**, have unit norm; often $K > n$ (redundant). The number of nonzero entries of $z$ is written $\|z\|_0$.

The **sparse coding** of $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ seeks a code $z \in \mathbb{R}^K$ with few nonzeros such that $y \approx Dz$, for instance
$$
\min_{z} \|y - Dz\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|z\|_0 \le s.
$$

This problem is NP-hard in general (Natarajan, 1995). Two families of methods approximate it: greedy pursuits and convex relaxation by the $\ell_1$ norm.
:::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 4.2 — Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP)]{.tag} Start from the residual $r = y$ and the empty support $S$. Repeat $s$ times:

1.  select the atom most correlated with the residual, $k^* = \arg\max_k |\langle d_k, r \rangle|$, and add it to $S$;
2.  recompute the coefficients on $S$ by least squares, $z_S = \arg\min_u \|y - D_S u\|^2$ (Proposition 0.3);
3.  update the residual $r = y - D_S z_S$, which is orthogonal to every selected atom.

Each iteration costs one product $D^\top r$ and one small least-squares problem (Pati and coauthors, 1993).
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Mutual coherence and spark]{.tag} The **mutual coherence** of a dictionary with unit-norm atoms is the largest correlation between two distinct atoms:
$$
\mu(D) = \max_{k \ne l} |\langle d_k, d_l \rangle| .
$$

The **spark** of $D$ is the smallest number of columns of $D$ that are linearly dependent.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Uniqueness and recovery under low coherence]{.tag} Let $y = Dx$ with
$$
\|x\|_0 < \frac12 \Big( 1 + \frac{1}{\mu(D)} \Big).
$$

Then $x$ is the unique sparsest representation of $y$. Moreover, two algorithms recover $x$ exactly (Donoho and Elad, 2003; Tropp, 2004):

-   OMP run for $\|x\|_0$ steps;
-   the $\ell_1$ problem $\min \|z\|_1$ subject to $Dz = y$.

::: proof
*Spark bound.* Take any $k$ columns; their Gram matrix has unit diagonal and off-diagonal entries of modulus at most $\mu$. By Gershgorin's theorem its eigenvalues are at least $1 - (k-1)\mu$, positive when $k < 1 + 1/\mu$. Such columns are independent, so $\mathrm{spark}(D) \ge 1 + 1/\mu$.

*Uniqueness.* If $Dx' = y$ with $\|x'\|_0 \le \|x\|_0$, then $D(x - x') = 0$ with
$$
\|x - x'\|_0 \le 2\|x\|_0 < 1 + 1/\mu \le \mathrm{spark}(D),
$$
so the columns used by $x - x'$ are independent and $x = x'$.

*Recovery.* The recovery of OMP and $\ell_1$ minimisation is proved in the cited papers; the key step for OMP is that, under the condition, the atom most correlated with the residual always belongs to the true support. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the union of the identity and the orthonormal Fourier basis in dimension $n$, $\mu = 1/\sqrt n$. With $n = 64$ the theorem guarantees recovery of any combination of at most 4 spikes and sinusoids (Exercise 10).

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Soft thresholding, ISTA and FISTA]{.tag} The proximal operator of $\tau \|\cdot\|_1$ is the **soft thresholding**

::: key
[Key result — soft thresholding]{.tag}
$$
S_\tau(u)_k = \mathrm{sign}(u_k)\, \max(|u_k| - \tau,\, 0).
$$
:::

For the lasso $F(z) = \frac12 \|y - Dz\|^2 + \lambda \|z\|_1$ and a step $1/L$ with $L \ge \|D\|_2^2$, the **ISTA** iteration is
$$
z^{k+1} = S_{\lambda / L}\Big( z^k - \tfrac1L D^\top (D z^k - y) \Big).
$$

It satisfies $F(z^k) - F^* \le L \|z^0 - z^*\|^2 / (2k)$. Its accelerated version **FISTA**, which adds a momentum step, reaches $2L \|z^0 - z^*\|^2 / (k+1)^2$ (Beck and Teboulle, 2009).

::: proof
*Proximal operator.* The problem $\min_v \frac12 \|v - u\|^2 + \tau \|v\|_1$ separates over coordinates.

For one coordinate, a minimiser $v > 0$ satisfies $v - u + \tau = 0$, so $v = u - \tau$, which is valid when $u > \tau$. Symmetrically, $v = u + \tau$ when $u < -\tau$.

Otherwise $0$ is optimal, since $|u| \le \tau$ means that $0 \in -u + \tau\,\partial|\cdot|(0)$.

*Iteration and rates.* ISTA is the proximal gradient method on $F$: a gradient step on the smooth part, whose gradient is $L$-Lipschitz, then the proximal operator of the $\ell_1$ part. The rates are those of the proximal gradient method and of its accelerated version; see Beck and Teboulle (2009) and [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Dictionary learning

Fixed bases (Fourier, wavelets) are universal but not adapted to a given signal. Dictionary learning fits the atoms to the data (Tošić and Frossard, 2011, in the official references).

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Dictionary learning]{.tag} Given training signals $Y = [y_1, \dots, y_N] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times N}$ — for instance windows cut from long series — solve
$$
\min_{D,\ Z} \ \frac12 \|Y - DZ\|_F^2 + \lambda \sum_{i=1}^N \|z_i\|_1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|d_k\| \le 1 .
$$

The norm constraint removes the scale ambiguity $(D, Z) \mapsto (\alpha D, Z / \alpha)$, which would otherwise drive $Z$ to zero. The problem is not jointly convex, but it is convex in $Z$ for fixed $D$ and in $D$ for fixed $Z$: one alternates between sparse coding and dictionary update.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Two dictionary updates]{.tag} Fix the codes $Z$.

-   **MOD** (Engan and coauthors, 1999): if $ZZ^\top$ is invertible, the unconstrained minimiser of $\|Y - DZ\|_F^2$ is

    $$
    D = Y Z^\top (Z Z^\top)^{-1},
    $$

    whose columns are then renormalised.

-   **K-SVD** (Aharon and coauthors, 2006): updating only atom $k$ and the row $z^k$ of its coefficients, with the error $E_k = Y - \sum_{j \ne k} d_j z^j$, the best choice is the leading singular pair of $E_k$:

    $$
    d_k = u_1, \qquad z^k = \sigma_1 v_1^\top .
    $$

::: proof
*MOD.* The objective separates over the rows of $Y$ and $D$: each row of $D$ solves a least-squares problem whose normal equations (Proposition 0.3) read $D\, ZZ^\top = YZ^\top$.

*K-SVD.* The objective restricted to atom $k$ is $\|E_k - d_k z^k\|_F^2$, the error of a rank-one approximation of $E_k$. By the Eckart–Young theorem, the best rank-one approximation is $\sigma_1 u_1 v_1^\top$, and $u_1$ has unit norm as required.

In practice $E_k$ is restricted to the signals that already use atom $k$, which keeps the codes sparse. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For millions of windows, the online algorithm of Mairal and coauthors (2010) updates the dictionary from mini-batches.

### Convolutional sparse coding

Cutting a long series into windows creates an artefact: a pattern that straddles two windows is coded twice, at arbitrary shifts. The convolutional model codes the whole series at once, with atoms that may appear at any time.

::: def
[Definition 4.8 — Convolutional sparse coding (CSC)]{.tag} Let $d_1, \dots, d_K \in \mathbb{R}^L$ be short atoms, $L \ll n$. A series $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is modelled as
$$
x \approx \sum_{k=1}^K d_k * z_k,
$$
where the **activation signals** $z_k \in \mathbb{R}^n$ are sparse: a spike of height $a$ at time $\tau$ in $z_k$ places a copy of $a\, d_k$ starting at $\tau$. The coding problem is
$$
\min_{z_1, \dots, z_K} \ \frac12 \Big\| x - \sum_k d_k * z_k \Big\|^2 + \lambda \sum_k \|z_k\|_1 .
$$

It is a lasso whose dictionary contains every shift of every atom: $Kn$ columns, highly coherent, but with a convolution structure that makes it tractable. Shifting $x$ shifts the activations: the representation is shift-equivariant.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — CSC in the Fourier domain]{.tag} With circular convolutions of length $n$, let $\mathcal{D}(z) = \sum_k d_k \circledast z_k$ and let $\hat d_k(\omega)$ be the DFT of the zero-padded atom $d_k$.

-   $\mathcal{D}$ acts frequency by frequency:

    $$
    \widehat{\mathcal{D}(z)}(\omega) = \sum_k \hat d_k(\omega)\, \hat z_k(\omega).
    $$

-   Its squared operator norm, the Lipschitz constant needed by ISTA and FISTA, is

    $$
    \|\mathcal{D}\|^2 = \max_\omega \sum_{k=1}^K |\hat d_k(\omega)|^2 .
    $$

-   The linear systems $(\mathcal{D}^* \mathcal{D} + \rho I) z = b$ of ADMM split into $n$ systems of size $K$, each with an identity-plus-rank-one matrix, solved in $\mathcal{O}(K)$ by the Sherman–Morrison formula (Wohlberg, 2015, in the official references).

::: proof
*Diagonalisation.* Theorem 0.5 applied to each term.

*Norm.* By Parseval and Cauchy–Schwarz at each frequency,
$$
\|\mathcal{D}(z)\|^2 = \frac1n \sum_\omega \Big| \sum_k \hat d_k \hat z_k \Big|^2 \le \max_\omega \Big(\sum_k |\hat d_k(\omega)|^2\Big) \sum_k \|z_k\|^2 .
$$

Equality holds when every $\hat z_k$ is supported at the maximising frequency (and its mirror frequency, for real signals) and proportional to $\overline{\hat d_k}$ there.

*Systems.* At frequency $\omega$, with $a = \overline{\hat d(\omega)} \in \mathbb{C}^K$, the matrix is $\rho I + a a^{*}$, and
$$
(\rho I + a a^*)^{-1} = \frac1\rho \Big( I - \frac{a a^*}{\rho + a^* a} \Big).
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

One FISTA or ADMM iteration therefore costs a few FFTs, $\mathcal{O}(K n \log n)$, instead of $\mathcal{O}(K n L)$ for direct convolutions. The block below codes a synthetic signal built from two atoms with FISTA.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, L, K = 1024, 32, 2
t = np.linspace(-1, 1, L)
atoms = np.stack([np.exp(-8 * t**2), np.sin(3 * np.pi * t) * np.exp(-3 * t**2)])
atoms /= np.linalg.norm(atoms, axis=1, keepdims=True)      # unit-norm atoms
Z = np.zeros((K, n))
for k in range(K):                                         # 5 activations per atom
    Z[k, rng.choice(n - L, 5, replace=False)] = rng.uniform(1, 3, 5)

Dh = np.fft.rfft(atoms, n)                                 # atoms in the Fourier domain
synth = lambda Z: np.fft.irfft((Dh * np.fft.rfft(Z, n)).sum(0), n)   # sum_k d_k * z_k
adj = lambda r: np.fft.irfft(np.conj(Dh) * np.fft.rfft(r, n), n)     # its adjoint
x = synth(Z) + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n)

lam, Lip = 0.2, (np.abs(Dh) ** 2).sum(0).max()            # Lipschitz constant (Prop. 4.9)
z = v = np.zeros((K, n))
tk = 1.0
for it in range(300):                                      # FISTA iterations
    u = v - adj(synth(v) - x) / Lip                        # gradient step
    z_new = np.sign(u) * np.maximum(np.abs(u) - lam / Lip, 0)   # soft threshold
    t_new = (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4 * tk**2)) / 2
    v = z_new + (tk - 1) / t_new * (z_new - z)
    z, tk = z_new, t_new
for k in range(K):
    found, _ = find_peaks(z[k], height=0.5)
    print(f"atom {k}: true {np.flatnonzero(Z[k])}, found {found}")
print("relative residual:", round(np.linalg.norm(x - synth(z)) / np.linalg.norm(x), 3))
```

The ten activation times are recovered exactly, for both atoms. The relative residual of 0.23 reflects the shrinkage of the amplitudes by the $\ell_1$ penalty; refitting the amplitudes by least squares on the detected support removes this bias.

::: note
[Note 4.10 — Convolutional dictionary learning in practice]{.tag} Learning the atoms alternates CSC with an update of the atoms under the constraint $\|d_k\| \le 1$, by projected gradient or ADMM. Initialising the atoms with random windows of the signal helps.

The learned atoms are prototypes of the recurring patterns, and the activations say when they occur. Pattern *extraction* and *recognition* (ch. 3) are thus solved together. For multichannel recordings such as MEG, Dupré la Tour and coauthors (2018) constrain each atom to be rank one across channels — a spatial pattern times a temporal waveform — which makes the atoms physically interpretable.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Sparse coding is NP-hard in general, but OMP and $\ell_1$ minimisation recover sparse codes exactly when the dictionary has low coherence.
-   The proximal operator of the $\ell_1$ norm is soft thresholding; ISTA converges at rate $1/k$ and FISTA at rate $1/k^2$.
-   Dictionary learning alternates sparse coding with MOD or K-SVD updates.
-   Convolutional sparse coding models a series as a few shifted atoms; the Fourier domain makes it cost $\mathcal{O}(Kn\log n)$ per iteration.
:::

## 5. Detecting changes and anomalies {#ch5}

A gait recording switches from walking to running, a machine drifts before failing, a sensor freezes for an hour. The first two are *changes*: the law of the series is different after some times. The last one is an *anomaly*: a value or a stretch that does not conform to normal behaviour. This chapter treats change-point detection as an optimisation problem, following the official review of Truong, Oudre and Vayatis (2020), and then the detection of anomalies.

### Change-point detection as penalised optimisation

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Segmentation and penalised criterion]{.tag} Write $y_{a..b} = (y_{a+1}, \dots, y_b)$ for a segment of a series $y_1, \dots, y_n$. A **segmentation** with $K$ change points is a set $\mathcal{T} = \{t_1 < \dots < t_K\}$, with the conventions $t_0 = 0$ and $t_{K+1} = n$.

Given a **cost function** $c$ that measures how homogeneous a segment is, the penalised criterion is
$$
V(\mathcal{T}) = \sum_{k=0}^{K} c\big(y_{t_k..t_{k+1}}\big) + \beta K .
$$

Change-point detection minimises $V$. A method is the choice of three elements: the cost, the search method and the penalty $\beta$ (or a known number $K$ of changes).
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Three cost functions]{.tag} For a segment of length $m = b - a$ with mean $\bar y_{a..b}$:

-   *quadratic* (changes in the mean):

    $$
    c_{L_2}(y_{a..b}) = \sum_{t=a+1}^{b} \|y_t - \bar y_{a..b}\|^2 ;
    $$

-   *Gaussian* (changes in mean and covariance): $c(y_{a..b}) = m \log\det \hat\Sigma_{a..b}$, with $\hat\Sigma_{a..b}$ the empirical covariance of the segment;
-   *kernel* (changes in distribution), for a positive definite kernel $k$:

    $$
    c_k(y_{a..b}) = \sum_{t=a+1}^{b} k(y_t, y_t) - \frac1m \sum_{s,t=a+1}^{b} k(y_s, y_t).
    $$

The first two are, up to constants, minus twice the Gaussian log-likelihood of the segment. With cumulative sums of $y_t$ and $y_t^2$, $c_{L_2}$ of any segment costs $\mathcal{O}(1)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — One change in the mean]{.tag} For $0 < \tau < n$, splitting $y_{0..n}$ at $\tau$ decreases the quadratic cost by
$$
c_{L_2}(y_{0..n}) - c_{L_2}(y_{0..\tau}) - c_{L_2}(y_{\tau..n}) = \frac{\tau (n - \tau)}{n} \big(\bar y_{0..\tau} - \bar y_{\tau..n}\big)^2 \ \ge\ 0 .
$$

Divided by the noise variance $\sigma^2$, this is twice the log-likelihood ratio of "one change at $\tau$" against "no change" for Gaussian data. It is also the square of the standardised CUSUM statistic at $\tau$, so its maximum over $\tau$ is the squared maximal CUSUM statistic of the classical offline test.

::: proof
This is the analysis-of-variance identity: total sum of squares = within-segment sum + between-segment sum. With $\bar y = (\tau \bar y_1 + (n - \tau)\bar y_2)/n$, the between part is $\tau(\bar y_1 - \bar y)^2 + (n - \tau)(\bar y_2 - \bar y)^2$.

Now $\bar y_1 - \bar y = \frac{n - \tau}{n}(\bar y_1 - \bar y_2)$ and $\bar y_2 - \bar y = \frac{\tau}{n}(\bar y_2 - \bar y_1)$. The sum is therefore
$$
\frac{\tau (n-\tau)^2 + (n - \tau)\tau^2}{n^2} (\bar y_1 - \bar y_2)^2 = \frac{\tau(n - \tau)}{n} (\bar y_1 - \bar y_2)^2.
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — Locating one change by hand]{.tag} Let $y = (0.1, -0.2, 0.0, 2.1, 1.9, 2.0)$. The gains of Proposition 5.3 for $\tau = 1, \dots, 5$ are
$$
0.94, \quad 3.20, \quad 6.20, \quad 2.80, \quad 1.24 .
$$

The maximum is at $\tau = 3$, between the third and fourth samples. The split is kept if its gain exceeds the penalty $\beta$; with a noise level $\sigma = 0.15$ and the BIC-type penalty $2\sigma^2 \log n \approx 0.08$ (justified in Note 5.9 below), it is kept by a wide margin.
:::

### Search methods

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Optimal partitioning (Jackson and coauthors, 2005)]{.tag} Let $F(0) = -\beta$ and, for $t = 1, \dots, n$,

::: key
[Key result — optimal partitioning]{.tag}
$$
F(t) = \min_{0 \le s < t} \Big[ F(s) + c(y_{s..t}) + \beta \Big].
$$
:::

Then $F(n) = \min_{\mathcal{T}} V(\mathcal{T})$, and the optimal segmentation is recovered by storing the minimising $s$ at each $t$ and backtracking from $n$. The cost is $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ evaluations of $c$.

::: proof
By induction, $F(t)$ is the optimal penalised cost of $y_{0..t}$. Let $s$ be the last change point of an optimal segmentation of $y_{0..t}$, or $s = 0$ if there is none.

The part of that segmentation before $s$ must be optimal for $y_{0..s}$; otherwise, replacing it would lower the total.

The total is therefore $F(s) + c(y_{s..t}) + \beta$, where the convention $F(0) = -\beta$ cancels the penalty of the first segment, and minimising over $s$ gives $F(t)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.6 — PELT pruning (Killick, Fearnhead and Eckley, 2012)]{.tag} Assume there is a constant $\kappa$ such that, for all $a < t < b$,
$$
c(y_{a..t}) + c(y_{t..b}) + \kappa \le c(y_{a..b}).
$$

If, at some time $t$, a candidate $s < t$ satisfies $F(s) + c(y_{s..t}) + \kappa > F(t)$, then $s$ is never the optimal last change point before any later time $T > t$, and can be removed from the candidate set.

::: proof
For $T > t$, the assumption with $(a, t, b) = (s, t, T)$ gives
$$
F(s) + c(y_{s..T}) + \beta \ \ge\ F(s) + c(y_{s..t}) + \kappa + c(y_{t..T}) + \beta \ >\ F(t) + c(y_{t..T}) + \beta .
$$

The candidate $t$ therefore does strictly better than $s$ at time $T$, so $s$ is never the minimiser. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $c_{L_2}$ one can take $\kappa = 0$, since splitting never increases the cost (Proposition 5.3). The result is exact: PELT returns the same segmentation as optimal partitioning. When the number of changes grows linearly with $n$, its expected cost is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ under mild conditions (Killick and coauthors, 2012).

::: note
[Note 5.7 — Approximate searches]{.tag} **Binary segmentation** finds the best single split (Proposition 5.3 for $c_{L_2}$), then recurses on both sides while the gain exceeds $\beta$. It costs about $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ but can miss a short segment squeezed between two large changes. *Wild binary segmentation* (Fryzlewicz, 2014) searches random sub-intervals to fix this.

**Window-based** methods slide two adjacent windows along the series and compare them. They are fast and easy to run online, but each change is judged locally. The official review of Truong, Oudre and Vayatis (2020) organises all these methods by cost, search and constraint.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.8 — The kernel cost in feature space]{.tag} Let $\Phi$ be the feature map of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of $k$, so that $k(u, v) = \langle \Phi(u), \Phi(v) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$. For a segment of length $m$ with mean embedding $\bar\mu = \frac1m \sum_t \Phi(y_t)$,
$$
c_k(y_{a..b}) = \sum_{t=a+1}^{b} \big\| \Phi(y_t) - \bar\mu \big\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2 .
$$

::: proof
Expand the square:
$$
\|\Phi(y_t) - \bar\mu\|^2 = k(y_t, y_t) - \frac2m \sum_s k(y_t, y_s) + \frac{1}{m^2}\sum_{s,s'} k(y_s, y_{s'}).
$$

Summing over the $m$ values of $t$, the last two terms combine into $-\frac1m \sum_{s,t} k(y_s, y_t)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The kernel cost is therefore the quadratic cost of the data mapped into $\mathcal{H}$. With a characteristic kernel, such as the Gaussian kernel, mean embeddings differ whenever distributions differ: the cost detects changes in variance or shape, not only in the mean (Harchaoui and Cappé, 2007; Arlot, Celisse and Harchaoui, 2019).

::: note
[Note 5.9 — Choosing the penalty and scoring a segmentation]{.tag} For $c_{L_2}$ and Gaussian noise of variance $\sigma^2$, each change adds two parameters (a location and a mean). A BIC-type penalty is therefore
$$
\beta = 2\sigma^2 \log n .
$$

The noise level can be estimated robustly from the differences: $\hat\sigma$ is the median absolute deviation of $y_{t+1} - y_t$ divided by $0.6745\sqrt 2$. The official review discusses other calibrations, including from annotated signals.

A segmentation is scored by the error on the number of changes, the Hausdorff distance between true and estimated change points, and a precision and recall in which an estimated change counts as correct within a margin of $M$ samples of an unmatched true one.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
means, lengths = [0, 2, 0.5, 3, 1], [200, 150, 250, 100, 300]
y = np.concatenate([m + rng.standard_normal(l) for m, l in zip(means, lengths)])
n = len(y)
S1, S2 = np.r_[0, np.cumsum(y)], np.r_[0, np.cumsum(y**2)]
cost = lambda a, b: S2[b] - S2[a] - (S1[b] - S1[a]) ** 2 / (b - a)  # c_L2(y[a:b])

def pelt(beta, min_size=5, prune=True):
    F = np.full(n + 1, np.inf)
    F[0] = -beta
    last, R, evals = np.zeros(n + 1, int), [0], 0
    for t in range(min_size, n + 1):
        ok = [s for s in R if t - s >= min_size]
        vals = np.array([F[s] + cost(s, t) + beta for s in ok])
        evals += len(ok)
        F[t], last[t] = vals.min(), ok[int(vals.argmin())]
        if prune:                            # Theorem 5.6 with kappa = 0
            R = [s for s in R if t - s < min_size] + \
                [s for s, v in zip(ok, vals) if v - beta <= F[t]]
        R.append(t)
    cps, t = [], n
    while t > 0:                             # backtrack the optimal segmentation
        t = last[t]
        cps.append(t)
    return [int(c) for c in sorted(cps)[1:]], evals

beta = 2 * np.log(n)                         # BIC-type penalty, sigma = 1
print("true change points:", np.cumsum(lengths)[:-1].tolist())
for prune in (False, True):
    cps, evals = pelt(beta, prune=prune)
    print(f"{'PELT' if prune else 'optimal partitioning':20s} {cps}  cost evaluations: {evals}")
```
